Fu's Fs statistic

Source: R/neutrality.R
fusFs.Rd

Computes Fu's Fs (Fu 1997), a test of neutrality based on the probability of observing at least the observed number of haplotypes given the estimate of theta from nucleotide diversity. Under the infinite-sites model: $$F_s = \ln\!\left(\frac{S'}{1 - S'}\right)$$ where \(S'\) is the probability of observing a number of haplotypes greater than or equal to the observed value, given \(\theta = \hat{\pi}\).

Usage

fusFs(S, n, theta_pi)

Arguments

S

Integer scalar. Number of segregating sites; the haplotype count is taken to be \(S + 1\) (see Details).

n

Numeric scalar. Sample size. As in tajimaD, do not use raw read depth: use an effective sample size that reflects the number of independently sampled genomes.

theta_pi

Numeric scalar. Theta estimated from nucleotide diversity (\(\hat{\pi} \times L\)).

Value

Numeric scalar. Fu's Fs, or NA with a warning in three cases: at \(S = 0\), where \(S' = 1\) and Fs is infinite; at theta_pi = 0 with \(S > 0\), where there is no diversity to condition on; and when \(S + 1 > n\), since the statistic uses \(S + 1\) as the number of haplotypes, which cannot exceed the number of sequences sampled.

Details

The haplotype count is not observed. Per-site calls cannot say how many distinct haplotypes a sample holds, so the function sets that number to \(S + 1\). Under infinite sites without recombination this is the largest number of haplotypes \(S\) segregating sites can produce, and it is usually far above the number present. The value therefore carries no haplotype information: it depends only on \(S\), \(n\) and theta_pi, the summaries Tajima's D already contrasts, and under neutrality it is pushed below 0, increasingly so as \(\theta\) grows. With \(n = 100\) and \(S\) and theta_pi at their neutral expectations, it is -1.46 at \(\theta = 2\) (\(S = 10\)), -7.00 at \(\theta = 5\) (\(S = 26\)) and -25.0 at \(\theta = 10\) (\(S = 52\)), where the expected numbers of haplotypes are 8.4, 15.7 and 24.4 rather than 11, 27 and 53; at \(\theta = 1\) (\(S = 5\)) it is -0.37, and at very small \(\theta\) it can be positive (+0.55 at \(\theta = 0.2\), \(S = 1\)). A negative value is therefore not evidence of population expansion or hitchhiking, and no fixed threshold calibrates it.

The probability is computed exactly, for every n, from Ewens' sampling formula, \(P(K = k) = |s(n, k)| \theta^k / \theta_{(n)}\), with the unsigned Stirling numbers of the first kind built in log space. \(S'\) is held below 1 - .Machine$double.eps, so the value cannot exceed about 36.

References

Fu YX (1997). Statistical tests of neutrality of mutations against population growth, hitchhiking and background selection. Genetics 147:915-925.

Examples

fusFs(S = 10, n = 100, theta_pi = 5)
#> [1] 3.014689
